content:
Hey, I was curious about to what extent these large AI-driven proofs, like Navier-Stokes and FLT, used similar sorts of Lean as in mathlib, vs their own style. So I put together these stats, and I thought I'd share them here if anybody else is curious.

https://lacker.io/leanstats/

The AIs seem fairly divergent from each other, there is not just an "AI style" vs a "human style", which is one thing I was wondering. There's a bunch of differences, like Claude loves to use haveI, whereas ChatGPT hardly ever does. There are some commonalities in the AI styles, like the AIs use a lot less simp. Those, to me, don't seem likely to be subject-matter related. Neither of the AIs are writing new tactics in any significant way here.

I think you could probably make a small model to do Pangram-style author identification if you so desired. Probably some data errors due to using plain string counting rather than a tokenizer so if you want perfectly accurate data you should redo.
Cool! I would be interested to see the results running on https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti !
all the code to generate this is at https://github.com/lacker/leanstats - probably not too hard to add more repos if you're curious

I would imagine that an expert in metaprogramming (or in this day and age, anyone with access to a frontier LLM) would be able to replace the string-based approach with a token-based one, which would probably be more robust. I think this is a very interesting investigation. Extensions could be: figuring out how dialects of an LLM change over time, figuring out which model is powering various other tools such as Aristotle/Gauss.

I guess one reason Tau Ceti is an interesting case is that it is (I think) using a combination of models to write code.

Here's ChatGPT running it on Tau Ceti

The reason I think it is interesting is that presumably the author / review prompts influence these stats. For instance one might hypothesize that Mathlib has high simp usage because humans get annoyed when things which are good simp theorems candidates are not tagged, while AI might be more willing to just look up untagged theorems as needed. Anyway Tau Ceti's share is 13.6% which is somewhere in between.

@Kevin Buzzard , indeed here is an implementation with metaprograms: https://github.com/AxiomMath/lean-metrics
And here is the outputs on a bunch of different repos: https://openreview.net/pdf?id=5xTutqw6LQ
